questions.stem: Why is the propan-1-ol added drop by drop into the cooled oxidising agent?

options.text: To control the exothermic oxidation and limit the alcohol's exposure, catching the aldehyde stage
options.explanation: Slow addition plus cooling keeps the reaction manageable and stops short where intended.

options.text: Because the alcohol is too viscous to pour
options.explanation: Propan-1-ol is a thin liquid; a pipette serves precision, not viscosity.
The iced bath cools; the dropwise rate controls exposure.

options.text: Because the full volume reacts explosively
options.explanation: With control the reaction is safe; portioning is precaution, not desperation.

questions.stem: Heating is done with an electric heater or water bath rather than a Bunsen burner because

options.explanation: Water baths here are set to warm, not cool.

options.text: Propan-1-ol is flammable, and naked flames ignite its vapours
options.explanation: The flame-free heating is a direct fire-safety measure.
Bunsens heat glass routinely.
The heater supplies heat only.

questions.stem: Oxidising propan-1-ol all the way to propanoic acid requires

options.explanation: More substrate does not advance oxidation; more oxidant contact does.
Reduction runs the opposite direction of the intended oxidation.

options.text: Refluxing with excess acidified dichromate so the aldehyde is re-oxidised
options.explanation: Extended contact with excess oxidant drives the second oxidation stage.

options.text: Distilling the aldehyde the moment it forms
options.explanation: That deliberately stops at propanal.

questions.stem: The product propanal is purified by

options.explanation: Filtration removes solids; the products are liquids.
Titration measures concentration, not purification.
Flame tests identify metal ions.

options.text: Distillation, collecting the fraction at propanal's boiling point
options.explanation: The volatile aldehyde distils ahead of higher-boiling species.

questions.stem: Anti-bumping granules are placed in the pear-shaped flask to

options.text: Promote smooth boiling during the heating stage
options.explanation: The granules provide nucleation sites that prevent violent bumping.
The granules are chemically inert.

options.text: Absorb the propanal as it forms
options.explanation: Absorption would destroy the product; the granules do not absorb.
No filtration happens in the flask.

questions.stem: Name the two organic products obtainable from oxidising propan-1-ol.
questions.modelAnswer: Propanal, the aldehyde, and propanoic acid, the carboxylic acid formed on further oxidation.

questions.stem: State the safety precautions attached to the heating stage.
questions.modelAnswer: Use an electric heater or water bath instead of a naked flame, because propan-1-ol is flammable, and keep the flask cooled during the addition.

questions.stem: Explain why the pear-shaped flask is cooled in an iced water bath before the alcohol is added.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxidation is exothermic and the alcohol is volatile, so starting cold absorbs the reaction's heat release and prevents uncontrolled boiling or vapour loss during the dropwise addition.

questions.stem: A student distils the reaction mixture and collects a fraction that gives a positive Tollens' test. Identify the fraction and state the apparatus change that would instead have delivered propanoic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: The Tollens-positive fraction is propanal, the aldehyde; obtaining the acid instead requires the reflux set-up with excess oxidant, retaining everything in the flask rather than distilling early.

questions.stem: Why must propan-1-ol be kept away from naked flames?

options.text: The alcohol is corrosive to burners
options.explanation: Corrosion is not the concern.

options.text: Its vapour is flammable and ignites readily at a flame
options.explanation: A Bunsen burner near the alcohol risks immediate fire.

options.text: The flame would boil the alcohol instantly
options.explanation: Boiling is controllable; ignition is the hazard.

options.text: The flame oxidises the alcohol dangerously
options.explanation: The dichromate does the oxidation; the flame's hazard is ignition.

questions.stem: Potassium dichromate requires careful handling because it is

options.explanation: Category nonsense; it is an ionic solid.
It oxidises alcohols precisely because it is an oxidant.
The oxidising power is the declared hazard requiring care.
Dichromate is an oxidising solid in solution, not a fuel.

questions.stem: Spillages of the reagents are dealt with by

options.explanation: Evaporation spreads the flammable vapour hazard.
Igniting a flammable spill is the opposite of safe.

options.text: Sweeping them into the bin dry
options.explanation: Dry disposal preserves both hazards.

options.text: Mopping up right away with plenty of water
options.explanation: Dilution removes both the flammable vapour source and the oxidising concentrate.

questions.stem: A fume cupboard is used for harmful alcohols because

options.text: Their harmful vapours must be drawn away from the chemist's breathing zone
options.explanation: The extract removes inhalation exposure at its source.

options.text: The alcohols react with laboratory air violently
options.explanation: No such violent reaction occurs.
The cupboard's role is extraction, not cooling.
Solubility is unaffected by the cupboard.

questions.stem: Which set of alcohols does the practical name as flammable and harmful?

options.explanation: The label contradicts that claim directly.
The named three all carry the flammable and harmful labels.
Water is not flammable; the named set is different.
That pair is not the practical's named set.

questions.stem: State the two personal-protection measures attached to the harmful alcohols.
questions.modelAnswer: Avoid contact with skin and avoid breathing the vapour, using a fume cupboard where needed.

questions.stem: State the handling rule for potassium dichromate in this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Its declared hazard is oxidising strength, so it is handled deliberately, and spillages are mopped at once with plenty of water.

questions.stem: Explain why diluting spillages with water reduces both the fire and the oxidising hazards.
questions.modelAnswer: Water dilutes the alcohol below its flammable vapour range and spreads the dichromate out of its concentrated oxidising state, so one response defuses the two separate hazards simultaneously.

questions.stem: During the practical, a few millilitres of propan-1-ol spill near a lit Bunsen burner. State the immediate actions in order and the reason for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Extinguish the burner first to remove the ignition source, then mop the spill with plenty of water to dilute the flammable liquid, and ventilate or use the fume cupboard to clear harmful vapour.
